findings.title: Recovery codes are handed to user storage in plaintext
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential JSON-serializes the raw recovery codes and passes that string as the UserCredentialModel value to user.credentialManager().updateCredential. The local fallback still uses the recovery-code credential provider, which persists only hashes via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues. When a user-storage provider accepts the update — including the new BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage, which stores input.getChallengeResponse() and later compares it with String.equals — the codes are stored and checked in cleartext. Recovery codes are bearer login secrets, so a read of that user-storage attribute or row is enough to authenticate as the user, and the hashing applied to locally stored codes is skipped entirely.

findings.title: Federated recovery codes are never consumed and cannot be removed
findings.body: One-time use for locally stored recovery codes happens inside RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid, which marks the presented code used before returning true. If user storage reports that it supports recovery-authn-codes, credentialManager().isValid is delegated to that storage and the local provider never runs, so Keycloak never records which code was used. The only follow-up is removeStoredCredentialById, and only when allCodesUsed() is true. That call deletes a local credential by id; it does not update or disable a federated credential, and allCodesUsed() stays false when the federated model does not track usage. A code that just authenticated the user remains valid and can be replayed, and using the whole set does not remove the federated credential or reliably force reconfiguration.

findings.title: Login form requires a credential model user storage was never given
findings.body: RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean loads the credential through RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, which prefers getFederatedCredentialsStream, then immediately calls Optional.get() and RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel. That parser needs credentialData and secretData in the hashed recovery-code format (algorithm, iterations, per-code hash, used flag) to compute the next code number. createRecoveryCodesCredential never writes that model; it only sends a JSON array of raw code strings. A provider that stores and returns that payload, or whose getCredentials default is empty, makes the optional empty or unparsable. Rendering the recovery-code page then throws NoSuchElementException or a JSON error even though isConfiguredFor is true, so the user cannot sign in. The same createFromCredentialModel call in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator runs after isValid succeeds and turns a valid code into an error before context.success().

findings.title: Storage double and new test never check one-time use
findings.body: BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid accepts a recovery code if it equals any stored raw code and does not delete or mark that code used. getCredentials then rebuilds a model with RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues, which hashes the raw list again and assigns a new id, so every read looks like a fresh unused set and the id does not match the credential saved in updateCredential. testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only signs in once with code index 0 and asserts the credential exists in user storage. It never checks that the used code is rejected, that the next prompt advances, that a wrong code fails, or that the local fallback still stores hashes, so the test passes while replay and the login-form credential contract stay broken.
